source.title: Accuracy on the wrong line: On the pitfalls of noisy data for out-of-distribution generalisation
source.authors: Amartya Sanyal; Ya-Xi Hu; Yaodong Yu; Yi Ma; Yi-Xin Wang; Bernhard Scholkopf

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments where noisy training data is interpolated and examines how training accuracy relates to in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy. Its focus is a refinement about noisy interpolation and distribution shift, not whether random labels yield chance test error.
record.gate_note: Most evidence concerns ID/OOD accuracy correlations and label-noise interpolation, rather than training error on completely random labels. It does not test shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs, and does not report whether networks learn real-label patterns before noisy labels. Noisy Colored MNIST is trained to zero training error, but its label noise rate varies and the test distribution is noiseless with a smaller spurious correlation. FMoW models are reported at 100% training accuracy in the noisy interpolated setting.
record.test_reason: Colored MNIST tests V4 over a limited noise range: the MLP reaches zero training error at η = 0, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.25, while Figure 3 shows decreasing ID accuracy. The main ID/OOD correlation findings concern a different claim. No experiment establishes fitting completely random labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: noisy interpolation together with nuisance features can reverse the usual positive ID/OOD accuracy relationship. The authors support this with image experiments, conditional theoretical bounds and synthetic linear simulations; larger noisy datasets can exacerbate the effect.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies the relationship between ID and OOD accuracy under label noise and nuisance features. Experiments use Colored MNIST MLPs, fine-tuned ImageNet-pretrained vision models on FMoW-CS, and synthetic linear classifiers; the paper does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with label-noise rate, whether training reaches interpolation, dataset size, and alignment between the learned classifier and the shift distribution. In FMoW, non-interpolated runs retain positive ID/OOD correlation; increasing label noise and dataset size worsens OOD accuracy in the synthetic linear setting.

fits_no_version.finding: ID and OOD accuracy become negatively correlated under sufficiently noisy interpolation with spurious features; noiseless and non-interpolating settings retain positive correlations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy interpolation with nuisance or spurious features can reverse the relationship between ID and OOD accuracy across model configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic logistic regression, larger noisy datasets improve ID accuracy while worsening OOD accuracy under the constructed nuisance-feature shift.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing dataset size can worsen distribution-shift robustness when fitting label noise increases nuisance-feature sensitivity and density.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), 2024
record.problems: The deep-model evidence is primarily plotted correlations without exact values or uncertainty estimates. FMoW results aggregate across many configurations and do not give model-specific accuracy values in the text. The experiments assess ID/OOD accuracy correlations, not chance test error on completely random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separate result rows were omitted. Figures report values graphically without exact textual numeric values; the rows record only the paper's stated qualitative outcomes.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance, and fitting with architecture and training hyperparameters unchanged.
Comparative convergence time for true and random labels and slowdown across corruption fractions. Absolute runtime descriptions do not test these comparisons.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The trajectory beyond η = 0.25 through complete randomization, convergence toward chance, and a direct decomposition of signal learning and noise memorization.
Whether weight decay, dropout and augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels, and whether removing them alone harms true-label generalization.
Learning order of real-label patterns and noisy labels during training.

record.verdict_notes: Missing coverage of V1 is not a scope limitation demonstrated by results. Remove both existing V1 verdicts. The FMoW interpolation groups are selected subsets, so their 100% training accuracy does not establish success for every listed architecture or configuration.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports fitting noisy labels and zero training error, including the FMoW setting with label noise probability 0.5. It does not establish the full V1 combination of completely random labeling, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
The paper does not report comparative training time for true versus random labels or convergence speed across label-noise fractions.
The paper does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The paper studies how label noise changes the relationship between ID and OOD accuracy, not whether training error stays perfect while test error rises steadily toward chance across noise fractions.

Regularization strength is varied in the synthetic linear experiments, but the paper does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels or whether removing them alone harms true-label generalization.
The paper does not examine learning order or compare when real-label patterns versus noisy or random labels are learned.

rows.subject: three-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Colored MNIST with label noise probability η and optimized to zero training error; test accuracy measured on a fresh noiseless test set with smaller spurious correlation.
rows.measure: ID and OOD accuracy as functions of model configurations and label noise
rows.baseline: η = 0: ID and OOD accuracy positively correlated
rows.value: At low label noise (Figures 3a and 3b), accuracies positively correlated; at higher label noise (Figures 3c and 3d), negatively correlated. Training error was zero.
rows.note: The paper describes plotted correlations but does not provide exact accuracy values in the text. Random labels across all training examples and chance test accuracy are not established.
rows.check: Separate noisy-label interpolation and declining ID accuracy from the ID/OOD correlation result. Zero training error is reported across the tested noise rates; Figure 3 shows ID accuracy declining across η = 0, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.25. The OOD set also changes spurious correlation, so its accuracy is not a clean measure of degradation from label noise alone.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on FMoW-CS with label noise probability 0.5; compared ID and OOD accuracy among training runs that fully interpolated the data.
rows.baseline: Noiseless interpolated models show positive ID/OOD correlation
rows.value: Noisy interpolated models show inversely correlated ID and OOD accuracy.
rows.note: Among various configurations, this model is one of the named architectures. The figure reports runs rather than a model-specific numerical summary.
rows.check: Figure 4a reports a pooled correlation among selected interpolating runs, not a ResNet-18-specific result. Noise probability 0.5 in this five-class task does not establish completely random labels. Neither a matched noise-rate trajectory nor architecture-specific interpolation success is reported.

source_check.correct: Figure 4a reports inverse ID/OOD accuracy correlation across pooled noisy interpolating runs from several architectures and configurations. ResNet-18 is among the architectures trained; no separate ResNet-18 correlation is reported.
source_check.problem: A pooled correlation is assigned to ResNet-18 without an architecture-specific result.

rows.subject: fine-tuned ImageNet pre-trained models (aggregate over more than 400 runs)
rows.size_stated: ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ResNet-101, DenseNet121; varied widths
rows.operation_detail: Compared noisy and noiseless FMoW-CS runs that fully interpolated the dataset.
rows.value: In the absence of label noise, ID and OOD accuracy are positively correlated.
rows.note: Text gives an aggregate qualitative result across configurations; it does not break this result down by model.
rows.check: Positive ID/OOD correlation without label noise does not measure any claim version. More than 400 models describes the overall experiment, not the number of noiseless interpolating runs.

source_check.correct: Figure 4b pools noiseless runs that fully interpolate the dataset; their number is not stated. More than 400 models describes the overall experiment in Section 2.2; Appendix B.4 describes nearly 400 models.
source_check.problem: The overall experiment's model count is incorrectly assigned to the noiseless interpolating subset.

rows.subject: fine-tuned ImageNet pre-trained models (aggregate over training runs)
rows.size_stated: ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ResNet-101, DenseNet121; varied widths
rows.operation_detail: Compared noisy FMoW-CS training runs that did not fully interpolate the data, including early stopping, stronger regularization, or smaller widths.
rows.baseline: Noisy interpolated models show inverse correlation
rows.value: ID and OOD accuracies remain positively correlated, but to a lesser degree than in the noiseless setting.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result across training runs; no model-specific values are stated.
rows.check: The result measures ID/OOD correlation in a subset selected for non-interpolation. Early stopping, stronger regularization and smaller widths are grouped together; this does not isolate regularization or demonstrate a failure to fit completely random labels.

rows.subject: ℓ1-penalised logistic regression classifier
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional data; one signal feature and 299 nuisance features
rows.operation_detail: Trained in synthetic simulations with label noise, varying dataset size; default noise rate 0.2 and dataset size 300 unless otherwise noted.
rows.measure: ID and OOD accuracy relationship as noise and dataset size vary
rows.baseline: η = 0: ID and OOD accuracy are linearly correlated
rows.value: As η increases, accuracies become nearly inversely correlated; ID accuracy increases with dataset size while OOD accuracy decreases in the noisy setting.
rows.note: This is a linear classifier, not a deep network; it demonstrates the paper's synthetic result on noisy interpolation and ID/OOD correlation.
rows.check: The subject is logistic regression, rather than the deep networks named by the versions, and the measure is ID/OOD correlation.

rows.subject: ℓ1-penalised logistic regression classifier
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional data; one signal feature and 299 nuisance features
rows.operation_detail: Synthetic linear simulation without label noise while varying dataset size.
rows.measure: OOD accuracy as dataset size increases
rows.value: OOD accuracy improves with increasing dataset size in the absence of label noise.
rows.note: Control condition contrasted with noisy interpolation.
rows.check: Noiseless logistic-regression generalization as dataset size increases does not measure any version.

rows.subject: ℓ1-penalised logistic regression classifier
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional data; one signal feature and 299 nuisance features
rows.operation_detail: Varied dataset size in the presence of label noise and measured accuracy and nuisance sensitivity/density.
rows.measure: ID accuracy and OOD accuracy versus dataset size
rows.value: ID accuracy increases with dataset size; in the noisy setting OOD accuracy decreases as dataset size grows.
rows.note: Evidence bears on interpolation of noisy labels but does not test all of V1's stated conditions.
rows.check: Logistic-regression accuracy versus dataset size is outside the versions' system and measure. It also substantially duplicates R9.

labels.condition: Colored MNIST MLPs, tested noise rates η = 0, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.25
labels.reason: R1: Section 2.1 and Appendix B.3 report training to zero error; Figure 3 shows declining ID accuracy across these noise rates. This supports V4 within the tested range. Fully random labels and degradation all the way to chance are untested.

relation.reason: The paper's own MLP experiments measure noisy-label interpolation and generalization across several corruption rates, bearing on the tested portion of V4.

tranche.reason: Colored MNIST provides a result on V4 in a setting with spurious color correlations: zero training error across the tested noise rates and declining ID accuracy. The paper's challenge to positive ID/OOD correlation concerns a different claim and does not warrant T5 for random_labels.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion paraphrase is supported. The principal result concerns ID/OOD correlation; the limited V4 evidence comes from Colored MNIST, with no complete-random-label experiment or numerical accuracy summaries stated in prose.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Noisy interpolated runs are reported at 100% training accuracy; the paper finds inverse ID/OOD accuracy correlation, consistent with successful fitting of noisy labels (R2–R6).

reader_labels.condition: Noisy Colored MNIST and synthetic linear setting
reader_labels.reason: These settings show noisy-label interpolation and changing ID/OOD relationships, but do not establish completely random labels, chance test error, or unchanged hyperparameters as specified in V1 (R1, R9, R11).
